messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 58
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: African
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Hairdresser
  trauma_type: Mugging or robbery
  pcl5: 72

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Being Criticised: Being criticised or corrected, Olfactory (Alcohol): Alcohol smell, Perceived Threat: People acting suspiciously
  Maladaptive Strategies: Self-Blame Rumination: I dwell on what I have done wrong, Suppress Thoughts: try hard not think about the trauma, Avoid People: avoid other people
  Memory: Visual Memories: My memories of the frightening event are mostly pictures or images., Memory Replay: My memories of the frightening event are like a film that plays over and over., Cannot Find Words: I know what happened but I am unable to find words to describe it

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Samuel Osei was fifty-eight years old, a hairdresser who had worked in the same shop in a busy strip mall for over two decades. The mugging happened on a Tuesday evening in late November, after he locked up for the night. A man stepped out from behind a dumpster as Samuel walked toward his car, shoved him against the brick wall, and pressed something hard and cold against his ribs. “Give me your wallet, old man. Don’t look at me.” The man’s breath was sour with alcohol—Samuel would never forget that smell, thick and sweet, mixed with the damp grease of the alley. He handed over his wallet, his phone, his keys, and stood frozen while the man ran. The whole thing lasted maybe forty seconds, but those seconds began playing in Samuel’s mind like a film loop, over and over, always the same images: the wall’s rough brick against his cheek, the glint of light on metal, the man’s shadow disappearing.

In the months that followed, Samuel tried hard not to think about it. He told himself to just move on, count his blessings that he wasn’t hurt worse. But the images kept coming, unbidden, and when they did he felt a sick lurch in his stomach. He could see the whole scene in vivid pictures—the dumpster, the alley, the man’s scuffed boots—yet when his wife asked what happened that night, he found he could not find words to describe it. His mouth would go dry, and he would shake his head. “I just can’t,” he would say, and she would stop asking, but her face crumpled with worry.

The alcohol smell became a landmine. A client came in one afternoon reeking of beer, and Samuel had to excuse himself to the back room, hands trembling, heart racing. After that, he started paying close attention to who walked through the door. People who moved too quickly, who kept their hands in their pockets, who glanced around the salon with what Samuel read as suspicious intent—he found himself making excuses to avoid them. He would say his next appointment was running late, or ask a coworker to take the client. He began to dread the sound of the bell above the door.

The hardest trigger was criticism. Samuel had always prided himself on his skill, but now a simple correction from a client— “a little more off the top, please” or “that’s not quite the style I wanted”—sent a rush of shame and anger through him. He heard it as an accusation, as if they were saying he had done something wrong, the same way he kept telling himself that if he had just walked faster, or taken a different route, the robbery would not have happened. He dwelled on what he had done wrong, replaying his own decisions in the alley: why had he parked so far from the door? Why had he not looked behind the dumpster? He turned the blame inward, hour after hour, until his mind felt worn thin.

To stop the cycle, Samuel avoided other people whenever he could. He stopped going to church, stopped meeting his old friends for coffee. He told his wife he was tired, that work was slow. But work was not slow—he was turning clients away. The salon owner noticed his absences and spoke to him gently, but Samuel felt the words like a reprimand. He came to believe that people could see his fear, that they judged him for it. He monitored every face, every tone, always on the lookout for the next threat or the next criticism.

By the time he called my office, his wife had begun making phone calls behind his back, he suspected. He came because he could not keep living like this—jumping at smells, replaying the film, hiding in the back of the salon. What he hoped for, he said quietly, was to stop feeling like he was still in that alley. What frightened him most was the possibility that the man with the alcohol breath would come back, or that he would never again feel safe in his own shop.
